definitions.definition: A made-up field that tries to connect physics and theology using math.
definitions.example: Like mixing science class and religion class into one subject.

definitions.definition: A difference or imbalance between two things that are otherwise similar.
definitions.example: A seesaw with one side heavier than the other.

definitions.definition: A number that represents how much truth a person is willing to accept.
definitions.example: Like a volume knob for how open you are to hearing something true.

definitions.definition: The physics theory that explains how quarks and gluons stick together inside protons and neutrons.
definitions.example: The rulebook for the glue that holds the center of atoms together.

definitions.definition: Stored energy that can be released later, like a stretched rubber band.
definitions.example: A ball held above the ground has potential energy because it can fall.

definitions.definition: Tiny particles that are the building blocks of protons and neutrons.
definitions.example: Like LEGO bricks for the center of atoms.

definitions.definition: The force that pulls quarks back together when they try to separate, like a rubber band.
definitions.example: The harder you pull two magnets apart, the harder they snap back.

definitions.definition: The rule that quarks can never be pulled apart alone; they always stay stuck together.
definitions.example: You can't have just one end of a magnet; it always has two poles.

definitions.definition: A fixed number that tells how strong a force is between particles.
definitions.example: Like a dial that sets how sticky two things are.

definitions.definition: The pull-back force in a relationship when people grow apart, like a rubber band of commitment.
definitions.example: The sadness you feel when a friend moves away.

definitions.definition: A number that represents the effect of someone choosing to break a relationship.
definitions.example: Like a subtraction from trust when someone lies.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; things tend to get messier over time.
definitions.example: Your bedroom gets messier on its own, but it never gets cleaner without work.

definitions.definition: The fact that time only moves forward because disorder always increases.
definitions.example: You can un-break an egg in a video played backward, but not in real life.

definitions.definition: A made-up idea that spiritual or moral disorder in a person tends to increase over time.
definitions.example: Like a bad habit that gets worse if you don't try to fix it.

definitions.definition: Energy added from outside a system to change it.
definitions.example: Pushing a swing from the outside to make it go higher.

definitions.definition: In Christianity, unearned help or forgiveness from God.
definitions.example: A free gift you didn't earn, like a surprise scholarship.

definitions.definition: A formula that measures how much information or surprise is in a message.
definitions.example: A coin flip has high Shannon entropy because you can't predict the outcome.

definitions.definition: A list of all possible outcomes and how likely each one is.
definitions.example: A dice roll has a probability distribution: each number has a 1 in 6 chance.

definitions.definition: A Greek word meaning 'Word' or 'reason'; in Christianity, it refers to Jesus as the divine reason behind creation.
definitions.example: Like the blueprint or logic that the universe was built from.

definitions.definition: A measure of how simple or complex a piece of information is, based on the shortest computer program that can produce it.
definitions.example: A repeating pattern like 'ABABAB' has low Kolmogorov complexity because it's easy to describe.

definitions.definition: A quantity that stays the same for all observers, even if they are moving at different speeds.
definitions.example: The speed of light is the same for everyone, no matter how fast you're going.

definitions.definition: A fixed distance between two events that combines space and time; all observers agree on it.
definitions.example: The 'distance' between two moments that everyone measures the same way.

definitions.definition: Einstein's theory that says the laws of physics are the same for all observers moving at constant speed, and the speed of light is always the same.
definitions.example: Time slows down for someone moving very fast compared to someone standing still.

definitions.definition: Something that does not change, even when other things around it do.
definitions.example: Your height changes, but your birthday is invariant.

definitions.definition: A made-up idea that there is a fixed truth about a relationship that both people can agree on.
definitions.example: Even if two friends remember an argument differently, something real happened between them.

definitions.definition: The time measured by a clock that is moving along with the thing being timed.
definitions.example: The time you experience on a spaceship, not what someone on Earth sees.

definitions.definition: A set of equations that convert measurements of space and time between two observers moving at different speeds.
definitions.example: A formula to translate what one person sees into what another person sees.

definitions.definition: The main equation of quantum mechanics that describes how a quantum system changes over time.
definitions.example: The rulebook for how tiny particles behave.

definitions.definition: A description of all the possible properties of a quantum particle at a given time.
definitions.example: Like a snapshot of everything a particle could be.

definitions.definition: The strange quantum property where a particle exists in multiple states at once until it is measured.
definitions.example: Schrödinger's cat is both alive and dead until you open the box.

definitions.definition: A formula that tells you the probability of finding a quantum particle in a particular state when you measure it.
definitions.example: Like odds for which side a quantum coin will land on.

definitions.definition: A made-up equation that tries to describe how faith changes over time, like quantum mechanics for belief.
definitions.example: Like a math formula for how hope grows or shrinks.

definitions.definition: The moment a quantum particle stops being in multiple states and becomes just one state when measured.
definitions.example: When you open the box, the cat is either alive or dead, not both.

definitions.definition: A type of radioactive decay where a neutron turns into a proton, releasing an electron and an antineutrino.
definitions.example: A tiny particle inside an atom changes into something else and shoots out a smaller particle.

definitions.definition: One of the four fundamental forces; it's responsible for certain types of radioactive decay.
definitions.example: The force that makes some atoms unstable and causes them to break apart.

definitions.definition: A particle in the nucleus of an atom that has no electric charge.
definitions.example: A neutral LEGO brick in the center of an atom.

definitions.definition: A positively charged particle in the nucleus of an atom.
definitions.example: A positive LEGO brick in the center of an atom.

definitions.definition: A tiny negatively charged particle that orbits the nucleus of an atom.
definitions.example: A tiny negative ball zipping around the center of an atom.

definitions.definition: A tiny, nearly massless particle that is the antimatter version of a neutrino, released in beta decay.
definitions.example: A ghost-like particle that comes out when an atom decays.

definitions.definition: A process where a quark changes from one type (flavor) to another, like a down quark becoming an up quark.
definitions.example: Like a red LEGO brick turning into a blue one.

definitions.definition: Atoms of the same element that have an unstable nucleus and decay over time, releasing radiation.
definitions.example: Atoms that are 'ticking time bombs' that eventually break apart.

definitions.definition: How fast a radioactive substance breaks down, measured by the number of decays per second.
definitions.example: How quickly a pile of unstable atoms is falling apart.

definitions.definition: A very advanced math method used in quantum field theory to predict how particles interact.
definitions.example: A super-complicated recipe for figuring out what tiny particles will do.

definitions.definition: A state where things are connected, consistent, and working together in an orderly way.
definitions.example: A choir singing in perfect harmony versus a crowd shouting randomly.

definitions.definition: A big formula that tries to combine all the laws of physics and spirituality into one equation.
definitions.example: The ultimate recipe for everything.

definitions.definition: A mathematical space where every possible position and state of a system is represented as a single point.
definitions.example: A map of every possible way a system can be arranged.

definitions.definition: A mathematical operation that adds up infinitely many tiny pieces to find a total.
definitions.example: Adding up the area of a shape by summing millions of tiny squares.

definitions.definition: An equation that describes how something changes over time or space using rates of change.
definitions.example: A formula that predicts how fast a population will grow.

definitions.definition: A system that changes over time according to fixed rules.
definitions.example: A bouncing ball whose path is determined by gravity and the floor.

definitions.definition: A system where each part depends on the others, and they all change together in a loop.
definitions.example: A video feedback loop where the camera shows the screen that shows the camera.

definitions.definition: A state where everything is balanced and nothing is changing anymore.
definitions.example: A seesaw perfectly level with two kids of equal weight.

definitions.definition: In Christianity, being saved from sin and its consequences, often seen as going to heaven.
definitions.example: Being rescued from a bad situation you can't fix yourself.

definitions.definition: A made-up equation that tries to combine all forces and spiritual laws into one formula.
definitions.example: The 'theory of everything' for both physics and faith.

definitions.definition: A mathematical expression that tells how well something is working or being used.
definitions.example: A percentage that shows how much of your phone's battery is actually powering the screen.

definitions.definition: A made-up mathematical limit that says only an infinite source of grace can save a soul forever.
definitions.example: The idea that you need an endless battery to keep a device running forever.

definitions.definition: The idea that without outside help, everything eventually falls into complete disorder.
definitions.example: A sandcastle will eventually be washed away by the tide unless someone keeps rebuilding it.

definitions.definition: A made-up theorem that claims the ultimate foundation of reality cannot be proven using the tools it provides.
definitions.example: You can't use a ruler to prove the ruler exists.

definitions.definition: A made-up rule stating that the most basic thing something rests on cannot be proven from inside that thing.
definitions.example: You can't prove the dictionary is correct by looking up words in it.

definitions.definition: A basic statement that is accepted as true without proof, used as a starting point for other reasoning.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: Rules that tell you how to logically move from one statement to another in a proof.
definitions.example: If A equals B and B equals C, then A equals C.

definitions.definition: A statement that follows easily from a theorem that has already been proven.
definitions.example: If you prove all squares are rectangles, a corollary is that all square corners are right angles.

definitions.definition: A famous math theorem that says a mathematical system cannot prove its own consistency.
definitions.example: A computer cannot check its own programming for errors without an outside program.

definitions.definition: So sure about something that you act on it, even if you can't prove it formally.
definitions.example: You are operationally certain the sun will rise tomorrow, even though you can't prove it.

definitions.definition: A situation where the universe seems to have a twist that is the opposite of what you'd expect.
definitions.example: The fire station burning down.

definitions.definition: Something made by humans, or in this context, something that is not the real thing but a byproduct.
definitions.example: A fossil is an artifact of a once-living thing.

definitions.definition: A series of logical requirements that the ultimate foundation of reality must satisfy.
definitions.example: A list of must-haves for the 'something' that created everything.

definitions.definition: Not made of matter or energy; not part of the physical universe.
definitions.example: A thought or an idea is non-physical.

definitions.definition: Something that does not depend on anything else for its existence; it just exists necessarily.
definitions.example: A necessary being that cannot not exist.

definitions.definition: Something that could either exist or not exist, depending on other conditions.
definitions.example: A chair is contingent because it depends on wood and a maker.

definitions.definition: Not limited by the rules of a formal system like logic or math.
definitions.example: A feeling or intuition is non-formal.

definitions.definition: Something that is the reason for its own existence; it doesn't need anything outside itself.
definitions.example: A foundation that holds itself up without any supports.

definitions.definition: The idea that everything must have a reason or cause for why it is the way it is.
definitions.example: There's a reason why your socks are on the floor, even if you don't know it.

definitions.definition: What kind of existence or reality something has.
definitions.example: The ontological status of a unicorn is 'imaginary'.

definitions.definition: Made real or concrete; given a specific form.
definitions.example: The idea of a chair is instantiated when someone builds one.

definitions.definition: The practice of defending a religious belief using arguments and evidence.
definitions.example: A lawyer defending their faith in court.
